Bentzinger CF.lab_name: Bentzinger Lab, Department of Pharmacology-Physiology, Université de Sherbrooke (Sherbrooke, Quebec, Canada)
Bentzinger CF.role: Muscle stem cell biologist at the Université de Sherbrooke who, as a PhD student in Basel, showed that mTORC1 but not mTORC2 is essential for healthy skeletal muscle
Bentzinger CF.sub: Professor, Department of Pharmacology-Physiology, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Université de Sherbrooke, and researcher at the CRCHUS (since 2016) · Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences, Lausanne (2014–2016) · postdoc, Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (2009–2013) · PhD, Biozentrum, University of Basel (2005–2009)
story: mTOR works in two complexes. mTORC1 needs the partner protein raptor, and mTORC2 needs rictor. Florian Bentzinger was first author of the 2008 Cell Metabolism study in this Atlas (BEN2008), done in Markus Ruegg's group at the Biozentrum in Basel with Michael Hall. The team deleted raptor or rictor only in the skeletal muscle of mice. Without raptor, the muscles changed their metabolism, lost oxidative capacity, became weak and developed muscular dystrophy, and the mice died early. Without rictor, the muscles stayed normal. This showed that mTORC1, not mTORC2, is the complex that muscle depends on, a result from mice that has guided later thinking about mTOR drugs and muscle.

Bentzinger did an MSc and then a PhD at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel (2005 to 2009). From 2009 to 2013 Bentzinger was a postdoc at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute in Canada, and from 2014 to 2016 worked at the Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences in Lausanne.

Since 2016 Bentzinger has been a professor in the Department of Pharmacology-Physiology at the Université de Sherbrooke and a researcher at its hospital research centre, the CRCHUS. The lab studies muscle stem cells and their niche, the surrounding tissue and extracellular matrix that tell the stem cells when to rest and when to rebuild muscle, and how these signals fail in aging and muscular dystrophy. The group has also developed a protocol for making muscle stem cells from induced pluripotent stem cells.

highlights.BEN2008: First author: showed in mice that losing raptor, not rictor, in skeletal muscle causes metabolic changes and muscular dystrophy.

Duran RV.lab_name: Centro Andaluz de Biología Molecular y Medicina Regenerativa (CABIMER), CSIC (Seville, Spain)
Duran RV.role: Cell biologist who showed that glutamine breakdown feeds amino acid signalling to mTORC1, and who now leads research on mTOR, glutamine metabolism and cancer at CABIMER in Seville
Duran RV.sub: Senior Researcher, Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), CABIMER, Seville · group leader, Institut Européen de Chimie et Biologie, INSERM U1218 and University of Bordeaux (PubMed affiliation 2015–2017) · postdoc, Michael N. Hall lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (2012) · doctoral work, Instituto de Bioquímica Vegetal y Fotosíntesis, University of Seville and CSIC (2006)
story: Cells check whether they have enough amino acids before they grow, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is the checkpoint. Raúl Durán was first author of the 2012 Molecular Cell study in this Atlas (DUR2012), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel. In cultured cells, glutamine together with leucine switched on mTORC1 by speeding up glutaminolysis, the breakdown of glutamine into alpha-ketoglutarate. Alpha-ketoglutarate then acted through the Rag GTPases, the switches that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome. The work linked a metabolic pathway that many cancer cells overuse to the main growth signal.

Durán started in a different field. A 2006 first-author paper from the Instituto de Bioquímica Vegetal y Fotosíntesis in Seville studied how electron-carrier proteins feed photosystem I in cyanobacteria. After the postdoc in Basel, Durán led a team at the Institut Européen de Chimie et Biologie in Bordeaux (INSERM and University of Bordeaux). There the group described 'glutamoptosis', a form of cell death caused when glutaminolysis runs unchecked during nutrient shortage and autophagy is blocked (2017).

Durán is now a Senior Researcher of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) at CABIMER in Seville. A 2026 paper from the group, with Durán as senior author, found that the FGFR1 receptor drives a metabolic rewiring that lets glioblastoma cells resist the chemotherapy drug temozolomide, and that blocking FGFR1 restored sensitivity in cells and mouse models.

highlights.DUR2012: First author: showed in cells that glutaminolysis, through alpha-ketoglutarate, activates Rag-mTORC1 signalling.

Robitaille AM.lab_name: Thermo Fisher Scientific (San Jose, California, USA)
Robitaille AM.role: Mass spectrometry scientist who, as a PhD student in Michael Hall's lab, used phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 switches on the cell's production of pyrimidines, and who now works on proteomics applications at Thermo Fisher Scientific
Robitaille AM.sub: Senior Product Applications Specialist, Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose · postdoc, Randall Moon lab, University of Washington, Seattle · PhD, Michael N. Hall lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel
story: To grow and divide, a cell must copy its DNA and make lots of RNA, and both need pyrimidines, a family of chemical building blocks. Aaron Robitaille was first author of the 2013 Science paper in this Atlas (ROB2013), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel. Using quantitative phosphoproteomics, a mass spectrometry method that measures thousands of phosphorylation sites at once, the team found 335 proteins whose phosphorylation depended on mTOR. One of them was CAD, the enzyme that runs the first three steps of making pyrimidines. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches CAD on through S6 kinase. The work, done in cultured cells, tied the main growth signal directly to the supply of DNA and RNA building blocks.

Robitaille did the PhD at the University of Basel in Michael Hall's laboratory and then moved to the University of Washington in Seattle as a postdoc in Randall Moon's lab, using quantitative proteomics to measure protein levels and protein partners and to find regulators of embryonic stem cell differentiation. The thread through this work is the use of mass spectrometry to follow how cells respond to their surroundings when they decide to grow or change identity.
Robitaille now works at Thermo Fisher Scientific in San Jose, California, as a Senior Product Applications Specialist for mass spectrometry and proteomics.

highlights.ROB2013: First author: used quantitative phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 activates pyrimidine synthesis through S6 kinase and CAD.

Jenoe P.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Jenoe P.role: Protein chemist who ran mass spectrometry and protein sequencing at the Biozentrum Basel for decades and contributed protein analysis to many mTOR studies from Michael Hall's lab
Jenoe P.sub: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation to 2022) · Department of Biochemistry, Biozentrum, University of Basel (1995)
story: Many discoveries about mTOR depend on identifying proteins and the phosphate tags on them, and that is the job of mass spectrometry. Paul Jenö is a co-author of the 2017 Cancer Cell study in this Atlas (GUR2017) from Michael Hall's lab. In a mouse model where too much mTOR signalling causes fatty liver that turns into liver cancer, the team found that mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, drives the production of fatty acids and sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking either kind of fat synthesis prevented tumours in the mice, and in human liver cancer samples high lipid synthesis went together with mTORC2 activity.

Jenö has worked on protein analysis at the Biozentrum since at least the 1990s. A 1995 paper with Jenö as first author, from the Department of Biochemistry, described a simple method to digest proteins inside polyacrylamide gels to obtain internal sequences, a step that became routine in protein identification. Later papers list Jenö at the Biozentrum's Proteomics Core Facility, usually together with Suzette Moes, on studies ranging from mTOR signalling to maternal blood markers of Down syndrome (2009) and prostate cancer (2022).

PubMed shows more than 100 papers under this name, many of them from Michael Hall's lab, including the 2013 phosphoproteomics study that linked mTORC1 to pyrimidine synthesis. A current position after 2022 could not be confirmed.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author: provided protein mass spectrometry for the mouse study showing that mTORC2 drives liver cancer through lipid synthesis.

Hagiwara A.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Hagiwara A.role: First author of a 2012 mouse study from Michael Hall's lab showing that liver mTORC2 tells the liver that the animal has eaten, by switching on sugar breakdown and fat production
Hagiwara A.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall group (at the time of the study, 2012)
story: After a meal, insulin tells the liver to stop making glucose and to start burning it and storing the extra as fat. Asami Hagiwara was first author of the 2012 Cell Metabolism study in this Atlas (HAG2012), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel, which asked what role mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, plays in that switch. The team deleted rictor, a core part of mTORC2, only in the liver of mice.

In fed mice without liver mTORC2, the kinase Akt lost its activating phosphate at serine 473, and the enzyme glucokinase and the fat-making regulator SREBP1c became less active. The liver kept making glucose while glycolysis (sugar breakdown) and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice developed high blood sugar and high insulin with low blood lipids. Putting an always-active form of Akt back into the liver cells restored these functions. The study, in mice and mouse liver cells, placed mTORC2 at the centre of the liver's response to insulin.
PubMed lists Hagiwara at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel on this paper. No other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, so the later career is not known.

highlights.HAG2012: First author: showed in mice that liver mTORC2 activates glycolysis and fat synthesis through Akt, glucokinase and SREBP1c.
